summary: No poll measured a British capitulation. The nearest analogue is the fall of France in May–June 1940. Third-term support for Roosevelt rose sharply then, and Gallup found voters would have preferred Willkie absent a European war, which suggests war shocks helped the incumbent. Opposition to entering the war stayed near 79%, and isolationist and ethnic (Irish, German, Italian) voters drifted away from Roosevelt. Group-level data are thin.

actor_positions.text: Franklin Roosevelt stayed silent on his re-election plans until the July 1940 Democratic convention.
Roosevelt campaigned on a promise that American soldiers would not be sent into foreign wars if he was reelected.
Wendell Willkie announced in early 1940 that he would accept the Republican nomination.
Willkie advocated aid to the Allies, especially Britain, and backed the president on a peacetime draft.
In the fall campaign, Willkie accused Roosevelt of secretly planning to take the nation into war.
Winston Churchill declared that Britain would keep fighting to the end.
As Germany invaded France, Robert Taft told a Kansas audience that America should concentrate on domestic issues.
Thomas Dewey and Arthur Vandenberg opposed any aid to Britain that might lead to war.
William Allen White chaired the Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies and argued that aid to Britain would keep the US out of war.
William Bullitt claimed that Germany would invade the US if Britain were defeated.

caveats: No poll measured an actual British surrender; all evidence comes from a world where Britain was still fighting.
The fall-of-France analogue cuts both ways: a rally to Roosevelt alongside about 79% opposition to entering the war.
No data by sex, citizenship or Black voters; Black voters in the Deep South were largely disfranchised.
1940 Gallup quota samples under-covered some groups.
The ethnic evidence is thin and confounded with the third-term issue; Italy would be among the victors in the scenario.
Several key claims rest on Wikipedia.

notes:
**Scope note.** I ran four searches. The evidence on 1940 opinion and the topline vote is reasonable. I found nothing reliable on breakdowns by sex, citizenship, Black voters, or region beyond a few poll fragments. I found no peer-reviewed work on the ethnic questions and none on the comparative-democracies question. Where that is so, I say so. Several sources below are Wikipedia, which I used only as a pointer or as a secondary check. Nothing rests on it alone, except where marked.

## 1. Direct evidence

**Nothing on record matches the scenario.** Britain never capitulated, so no poll measured a world where it had. The nearest evidence is polling on a hypothetical British defeat and on opinion during the fall of France.

**Expectations of a British defeat.**
- In May 1940 Gallup asked which side would win and whether the US would enter the war. It also asked whether Germany would invade the US if Britain were defeated, citing Ambassador Bullitt's claim that it would. These are Gallup items from interviews on 5–10 May 1940. [S4] The published fragment I found does not give the results.
- By 5–10 September 1940, Gallup's "which side will win" item showed 43% saying England and 17% saying Germany. [S4] That is the nearest figure I found to a measure of expectations. The remainder is cut off in the excerpt.
- Gallup's December 1940 survey asked whether Germany and Italy would attack the US within ten years if they defeated Britain. It also asked whether US safety depends on England winning, and whether people would rather see Britain surrender than see the US enter the war. [S2] The excerpt did not return the totals. Those would be the closest direct measure of the scenario, but they date from after the election.
- In the same December survey, 65% of one voter group said US safety depends on England winning. [S2] The excerpt does not make clear whether that group is Roosevelt or Willkie voters. Check the original.

**Shift after the fall of France.**
- Before France fell, opinion was strongly against intervention. In February 1940, 77% opposed declaring war even if Germany appeared to be defeating England and France. [S1]
- As late as June, only 35% said the US should risk war to help Britain. After France fell and the Luftwaffe began bombing Britain, a September 1940 poll found 52% in favour. [S8] That is a gain of about 17 percentage points over roughly three months. The Gallup series on the teachingamericanhistory.org page shows 48% for keeping out and 52% for helping England [S1] on this question.
- Support for staying out of the war itself stayed high. As France and other western European nations fell, 79% said they would vote to stay out of the war. [S7]
- Reading the two together: people moved toward aiding Britain, but not toward fighting. That pattern fits both the Roosevelt and Willkie platforms.

**Effect on vote intention and the incumbent.**
- Support for a Roosevelt third term rose from 40% in August 1939 to 46% in October 1939 and then 57% in May 1940. It held at that level in June. [S24] That is a gain of 11 points in the weeks after the Low Countries invasion began.
- Gallup wrote in June 1940 that third-term sentiment rose sharply when the invasion began on 10 May. [S24]
- Scholars treat the war as decisive for Roosevelt's candidacy. One account says the international situation convinced Roosevelt to run and made the public willing to support a third term. [S10]
- Some evidence runs the other way, for isolationism or the challenger. Gallup found that without a war in Europe, voters preferred Willkie. [S16] In Gallup's own telling, 53% would have preferred Willkie if there were no war in Europe. [S32]
- On defence, in November 1940 voters preferred Roosevelt to Willkie 61% to 39% on strengthening national defence. [S1] The same source reports 60% to 40% for Roosevelt over Willkie if the US got into the war. Both figures come from respondents with an opinion.
- Roosevelt's lead was not stable. Gallup polls showed him roughly level or behind in July and August. Their lead then grew in September, to between 5 and 8 points. [S16] The post-France bump therefore did not translate straight into a lead.

**Which groups moved.** Group-level data on the shift are thin. What I can report:
- Party and region among Republicans: Willkie's "all aid short of war" stance won the support of many East Coast Republicans who disagreed with isolationist party leaders in Congress. [S16] That implies a regional split inside the GOP.
- In December 1940, Willkie voters in New England and the Middle Atlantic backed "help England" 60% to 40%. [S2] Compare that with the East Central region in 1941, below.
- In an April–October 1941 Gallup item, "yes" was 41% in New England and the Middle Atlantic, against 35% in the East Central region. [S31] I don't have the question wording, so I can't tell which policy it covers.
- I found nothing by sex, citizenship status, or Black voters. Do not infer those from the sources above.

## 2. Analogues

**The 1940 results (nearest in time and place).**
- Roosevelt won 54.8% of the popular vote to Willkie's 44.8%, carrying 38 of 48 states with 449 of 531 electoral votes. [S10]
- His margin fell below 1936's 60.8%, partly because of weaker support among isolationists, especially in the Midwest, and among Irish, German and Italian Americans unhappy about foreign policy. [S10] That is a drop of about 6 percentage points from 1936.
- Within the North, Roosevelt won 87% of the Jewish vote, 73% of Catholics and 61% of non-members; all the major Protestant denominations had majorities for Willkie. [S16] (Wikipedia; treat as a pointer.)
- On class, white-collar and middle-class urban voters backed the Republican while working-class voters went for Roosevelt. [S16]
- Outside the South and the big cities, the Solid South gave Roosevelt 78%, the 106 largest cities 61%, and Willkie won small cities, towns and rural areas with 53%. [S29] The Starting Points source is an educational web publication, not peer-reviewed.
- Polls had the race closer than it finished. The final Gallup poll showed 51.1% to 47.4%, against a result of 54.7% to 44.8%. [S16] Gallup's later Coronet article claimed the poll was the most accurate state-by-state poll in history. [S32]

**Ethnic voters and Axis successes.**
- The only direct evidence I found is the 1940 voting pattern itself, summarised above. Some accounts note that Willkie also did well in areas with many voters of Italian, German or Irish birth or ancestry. [S11]
- I found no reliable source on how those groups reacted specifically to Axis military successes. The Irish case does show a link to neutrality. A 1940 Roosevelt address asked Irish listeners what would become of Ireland if Germany won. [S13] That is a speech, not a measure of reaction, and it comes from an undergraduate honors thesis. Both are weak evidence.
- Gallup's September 1940 survey did record the country of parents' birth. It covers who would win, keeping out versus helping England, and opinion of Roosevelt and Willkie. [S28] The Roper Center holds the microdata (Study 31087193). That is the best route to group-level figures.
- Census-based point: most German- and Italian-born civilians in the US in 1941 had already received US citizenship. [S15] So these groups mostly were voters, not non-citizens.

**Other democracies under wartime emergency.**
- I found no reliable comparative evidence on whether wartime emergencies produce a rally or a turn against sitting governments.
- The general rally literature is mostly about US presidents. It describes increased short-run support for governments or leaders in international crises. [S22] One example given is Roosevelt's Pearl Harbor bump. The Wikipedia article says approval went from 72% to 84%, a gain of 12 points. [S22] That is a Wikipedia summary, not a primary source.
- Rally effects are not guaranteed. The lower the pre-crisis approval, the larger the usual increase. [S22] Rallies also tend to fade, so the timing of the shock matters. A UK or Canadian comparison would need a separate search, and I did not find one.

## 3. Named people

- **Franklin Roosevelt.** He stayed silent on his re-election plans until the July 1940 Democratic convention. [S24] He promised no involvement in foreign wars if reelected. [S16] In the campaign he said: "Your boys are not going to be sent into any foreign wars." [S10] After the election, he said in a fireside chat on 29 December 1940 [S13] that the US must be the "arsenal of democracy" (the speech is cited in the Irish thesis). He later authorized US ships to shoot German vessels on sight, after the September 1941 Greer incident. [S3]
- **Wendell Willkie.** He announced in early 1940 that he would accept the nomination. [S20] He was an outspoken advocate of aid to the Allies, especially the UK. [S16] He also backed the president on a peacetime draft. [S20] In the fall he accused Roosevelt of secretly planning to take the nation into war. [S16] That charge did cut into Roosevelt's support. [S16]
- **Winston Churchill.** On 4 June 1940 he said Britain would "go on to the end". [S21] Per a VOA account, he later warned Roosevelt that Britain could not fight alone much longer. [S12] That account is a general-audience source.
- **Robert Taft, Dewey, Vandenberg.** As blitzkrieg hit France in May 1940, Taft told a Kansas audience that America should concentrate on domestic issues. [S16] Dewey and Vandenberg opposed any aid to the UK that might lead to war. [S16] (Wikipedia.)
- **William Allen White.** He chaired the Committee to Defend America by Aiding the Allies, and said aid to Britain was meant to keep the US out of the war. [S8]
- **William Bullitt.** The May 1940 Gallup poll cited his claim that if Britain were defeated the Germans would invade the US. [S4]

## 4. Limits

- **No poll covers an actual British surrender.** Every figure above comes from a world where Britain was still fighting. A capitulation would be a different shock from the fall of France, and people would reason about it differently.
- **The fall-of-France analogue cuts two ways.** Third-term sentiment rose, which looks like a rally. Opposition to war also stayed near 79%. A scenario where Britain falls alone could have fed either a rally to Roosevelt or a push toward isolation. The sources don't settle which.
- **Opinion-poll limits.** Gallup in 1940 used quota samples. They are known to have under-covered some groups, and I have no figures for Black or non-citizen respondents. Black voters in the Deep South were largely disfranchised in 1940. I did not find a source on that here, so I am not stating a number.
- **The ethnic evidence is thin.** The only group-level figure is the 1936–1940 comparison. It also reflects the third-term issue and German or Italian ties. The Irish-American source is a thesis and does not measure votes.
- **The comparative-democracy question is unanswered** in my sources, so I can offer no analogue for it.
- **Case-specific caveats.** The Italian-American case is further muddied because millions of US citizens in 1940 were Italian-born [S14]. In the scenario, Italy would be among the victors. In 1940 itself Italy only entered the war in June.
- **Suggested next step.** The Roper Center's Gallup microdata, especially #1940-0209 (September 1940), could give parent-birthplace and region breakdowns. The Gallup volumes (Gallup, *The Gallup Poll: Public Opinion 1935–1971*, vol. I [S31]) may also contain them.
prompt:
Scenario for the 1940 United States presidential election (election day 1940-11-05).
A reader asked: "america loses ww2".
As modelled: The United States was not yet at war in November 1940, so the nearest version of an American defeat is this: Britain loses the Battle of Britain and capitulates in October, leaving the country to face a victorious Germany, Italy and Japan alone.
Kind of change: issue. Populations it reaches first: every voter.
Include how the same groups swung, by how much, when comparable issues or shocks hit nearby elections.

Questions to answer:
- How did American public opinion polls in summer 1940 measure expectations of a British defeat, and how did they shift after the fall of France?
- Did the fall of France in June 1940 move voters toward the incumbent administration or toward isolationist positions, and which groups moved most?
- How did German-American, Italian-American and Irish-American voters react to Axis military successes in 1940?
- Do wartime emergencies in other democracies show a rally to sitting governments, or a turn against them?

Groups the simulation distinguishes: men and women; native-born white, naturalized immigrant, non-citizen immigrant and Black adults; the Northeast, Midwest, South (the eleven former Confederate states), border states and West. Evidence by these groups is most useful.
